(b) structure of chromosome during mitosis (anaphase stage)
a. Chromatid

During metaphase stage during mitosis, each chromosome comprises two identical structures called chromatids, each containing a single DNAmolecule. These chromatids are attached at the centromere that separate during anaphase while moving to opposite poles. b. Chromonema (ta)

During prophase stage of mitosis, chromosomes appear in the form of thin filaments called chromonemata (Vejdovsky: 1912). A chromonema is an early stage of a chromatid, so both terms refer to the same structure: a single linear DNAmolecule with associated proteins. Chromonemata are the part of chromosomes that bear gene. c. Chromomere Chromomeres are regions of tightly folded DNA that appear like a cluster of bead of chromatin that can sometimes be observed on interphase. They are especially visible in polytene chromosomes (chromosomes which have undergone multiple rounds of DNA replication without cell division), where they align side by side to form chromosome beads. At metaphase, chromosomes are tightly coiled, and chromomeres are no longer visible. d. Centromere (Primary constriction)

The chromosomes possess a constricted region called centromere or primary constriction where two sister chromatids are attached. The position of the centromere is constant for a particular chromosome. The structure and function of the centromere is different from that of the rest of the chromosome. It is functional during cell division. Kinetochore is a trilaminar plate/disc situated upon the primary constriction or centromere.

The position of the centromere varies in different chromosomes based on which
chromosomes are classified into four types. They are: (a) telocentric, (b) acrocentric,
(c) sub-metacentric, and (d) metacentric chromosomes.

e. Nucleolar organiser (secondary constriction I) The constriction near one end of chromosome that induces the formation of nucleolus is called nucleolar organizer.

f. Secondary constriction (II) In addition to the primary constriction or centromere, the arms of the chromosomes may show one or more secondary constriction (called secondary constriction II). These constrictions are different from nucleolar organisers (called secondary constriction I). It represents the site of breakage and subsequent fusion.

g. Satellite Sometimes chromosomes possess round, elongated, knob-like extensions called satellites. It is the part of chromosome beyond the nucleolar organizer that does not change it shape and size. Chromosomes bearing satellites are called Sine Acid Thymonucleinico (SAT) - chromosomes (without thymonucleic acid or DNA).

h. Telomere (G., telo = for; meros = part) The tips of chromosomes located at the terminal end after Secondary Constriction II are called telomeres. The telomeres are different in structure and composition from the rest of the chromosome. It has a unique property of preventing the ends of the chromosome from sticking together.

Functions of chromosomes 1. Chromatin fibers contain DNA which acts as a genetic material. 2. They control the synthesis of structural as well as enzymatic proteins. 3. The changes in DNA cause mutation.
